99d82593-9d49-4752-bd19-5df838dd2f2e.one_liner: Eurodollar University's Jeff Snider and Steve Van Metre argue an energy shock is squeezing consumers and producing 2022-style front-loaded demand that will roll over into recession -- useful macro/recession-risk background for a rates desk, but no direct repo, funding, or credit content.
99d82593-9d49-4752-bd19-5df838dd2f2e.recap: The hosts revisit Pepsi's earlier price cuts, made to win back consumers priced out by ~$7 bags of chips, which failed to lift volumes; Pepsi is now signaling price increases again as energy and input costs rise, a reversal they expect to fail too. Kroger has pulled Red Bull and Borshead products in a supplier pricing standoff, framed as a marketing play to position itself as consumer-friendly. The hosts read these as symptoms of a broader energy shock (tied to the Iran conflict and rising diesel/fuel costs) that businesses are slow to accept because official narratives, including Fed governor Kevin Warsh's comments on a resilient labor market, understate consumer strain. They argue the August-September surge in retail sales and S&P Global PMIs is not organic strength but panic buying/front-loading ahead of expected price and rate increases, directly analogous to the 2022 inventory-and-demand cycle that preceded a US manufacturing recession and a full European recession. Supporting evidence cited includes falling University of Michigan consumer sentiment (especially the forward-looking component), PCE growth persistently falling behind trend, weak consumer discretionary stock performance, subdued wage growth and hours worked, and anecdotal traffic data (light Friday-night traffic near Disney in Orlando). The conclusion: this is the classic energy-shock-precedes-recession pattern, with consumers pulling back at the margin even though headline data looks resilient.

a1b3c167-fe8d-4705-a656-758f93b199bb.implications: For a repo/financing desk, the Riksbank's certificate/deposit-rate structure and its ability to toggle between ample and scarce reserves within a week is a live case study for how the Fed's own demand-driven reserve-regime debate (ample reserves, repo facility usage, reserve demand reduction) could evolve; the QE-threshold argument (capital losses, fiscal entanglement, ratchet effect) is directly applicable to ongoing US debate about using Fed balance-sheet tools to cap long-end Treasury yields.

a1b3c167-fe8d-4705-a656-758f93b199bb.one_liner: The Riksbank governor lays out, in unusual operational detail, a demand-driven corridor/reserve system and a hard-learned high bar for future QE — directly relevant lessons for anyone watching the Fed's own reserve-regime and balance-sheet debates.
a1b3c167-fe8d-4705-a656-758f93b199bb.recap: David Beckworth interviews Riksbank governor Erik Thedéen on the history and operations of the world's oldest central bank. After tracing the bank's founding in 1668 and its parliament-based governance (an executive board of five voting equally on rates, overseen but not directed by a politically-appointed council), the conversation turns to the Riksbank's operating framework. Thedéen describes a demand-driven corridor system: the deposit rate sits 10bp below the policy rate while one-week certificates pay the full policy rate, so banks voluntarily choose how much to park in certificates versus deposits (currently banks leave roughly SEK 100bn on deposit despite the lower rate, valuing liquidity access). Certificates can be sold back or repoed within days, letting the system swing between ample and scarce reserves inside a week, and the Riksbank has now largely wound down its domestic bond holdings via QT. The core segment covers Thedéen's June speech setting a high threshold for future QE: financial-stability QE (e.g., 2022 corporate bond turmoil, COVID) remains a live tool, but QE for inflation purposes is now viewed skeptically because Swedish borrowing is mostly variable-rate (blunting transmission), and because bond-buying created mark-to-market losses that forced the Riksbank to ask parliament for capital injections — an interaction with fiscal policy he sees as a direct independence risk. To avoid repeat capital asks, the Riksbank got parliament to approve a zero-interest reserve requirement on banks as a stable non-seigniorage revenue source. The episode closes with a discussion of Sweden's advanced but now-stalled digital payment adoption (cash down from 40% to 5% of purchases since 2010), a legislative push to keep cash usable at grocery stores, and skepticism that dollar or euro stablecoins threaten the krona given Sweden's fiscal/institutional credibility.
terms: QE -- quantitative easing, central bank purchases of bonds to inject liquidity/lower long-term rates
QT -- quantitative tightening, the reduction of a central bank's balance sheet via runoff or asset sales
OIS -- overnight index swap, a derivative referencing an overnight rate used to gauge policy-rate expectations
AML -- anti-money laundering, regulatory checks on financial transactions
DLT -- distributed ledger technology, the shared-database infrastructure underlying tokenized settlement systems
